question: Did the risk of a motorist being killed per mile driven in NYC decline from 2013 to 2025? Make a chart and answer based on this crash data.

options.denominator: none; absolute count of reported motorist deaths
options.reason: A careful analyst might choose the direct annual death count to see whether the total recorded toll changed, without implying an exposure-adjusted rate.
options.answer: Reported motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, but this crash data cannot show whether per-mile risk declined.
options.interpretation: This framing addresses whether the annual number of motorist deaths recorded in NYC crashes fell: it shows 110 deaths in 2013 versus 81 in 2025, with a peak of 139 in 2020. It is defensible as a direct count of the recorded toll, but it leaves risk per mile unanswered because the file has no miles-driven exposure. The check found 2,132,218 planned rows, no missing crash dates and no missing or negative motorist-killed values, so no rows were excluded; zero-death values were kept, and each year had records on both date boundaries although within-year continuity was not evaluated. The checked row count fell from 203,742 in 2013 to 85,546 in 2025, so this count reflects changing reported-crash volumes as well as deaths.

options.metric: percentage of included reported crashes with number_of_motorist_killed >= 1, by year
options.denominator: all police-reported NYC crashes in that year with an observed, nonnegative number_of_motorist_killed value
options.reason: A careful analyst might choose the share of reported crashes with a motorist death to compare fatality frequency relative to the crash records in each year.
options.answer: The share of reported crashes with at least one motorist death rose from 0.0501% in 2013 to 0.0877% in 2025, so this crash-level measure did not decline; per-mile risk is not measured.
options.interpretation: This framing addresses how often a reported crash included at least one motorist death: the share rose from 0.0501% in 2013 to 0.0877% in 2025, rather than declining. It is defensible as a crash-level prevalence measure because its denominator is all eligible crash records in that year, but it does not measure an individual's or a mile-driven's risk. The check found 2,132,218 planned rows, no missing crash dates and no missing or negative motorist-killed values, so no rows were excluded; zero-death records were retained as non-events, and each year had records on both date boundaries although within-year continuity was not evaluated. Eligible crash records declined from 203,742 in 2013 to 85,546 in 2025, and the file cannot establish whether changing crash-record volume reflects changes in exposure, reporting, or both.

answer:
1. The annual count of reported motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, but this data cannot establish whether risk per mile declined ([chart](out/option_1.png)).
2. The share of reported crashes with at least one motorist death rose from 0.0501% to 0.0877%, so this crash-level measure did not decline, while per-mile risk remains unknown ([chart](out/option_2.png)).
